modules.title: Module 1. People and people. Me at school. My school. My class

lessons.title: Me at school and in class. My school is the people around me. Professions in a modern school

exercises.label: The school community: who helps and how
exercises.text: A school works because many people cooperate. Teachers help pupils learn, librarians find useful sources, psychologists support emotional well-being, and medical staff look after health. Cooks prepare meals, while support staff keep rooms clean and equipment working. Read the description and draw a school community map: put “Pupil” in the centre and add at least five professions around it. Next to each one, describe a situation in which you would need that person’s help.
questions: Who would you ask if you could not find a book for a project?
How do the cook’s and cleaner’s work affect learning?
Write two ways to thank school staff.

exercises.label: A short survey about feeling comfortable in class
exercises.text: Work in pairs to find out what helps classmates feel part of the community. Write three neutral questions about cooperation, help and learning comfortably. With their agreement, ask five pupils without recording their names. Count repeated answers and suggest one shared action for the class, such as exchanging book recommendations each week. Explain who could help organise this action and how you would check its usefulness.
questions: Which three questions will you ask?
Which answer appeared most often?
Why do five answers not represent the views of every pupil in the school?

lessons.title: Learning conditions and tools: how they have changed. School energy efficiency

exercises.label: How learning tools have changed
exercises.text: People recorded knowledge on different materials, later made wide use of printed books, and now supplement them with digital tools. A printed textbook can be read without electricity; a digital one makes it easy to search for words, enlarge text and play videos. A digital device needs energy, so using it does not automatically save energy. Choose one learning task and explain how to do it with a book and with a tablet. Compare convenience, accessibility and electricity use.
questions: Give two advantages of a printed textbook.
For which task is searching a digital text useful?
Why should pupils’ needs guide the choice of learning tools?

exercises.label: How much energy does lighting use?
exercises.text: Imagine two lamps that provide the same useful lighting: lamp A has a power of 60 W and lamp B a power of 10 W. In 5 hours they use 300 Wh and 50 Wh respectively, because energy equals power multiplied by operating time. For six identical lamps, multiply each result by six. Calculate the figures in your notebook, compare the totals and explain the difference. These are practice data: adults with suitable expertise choose and replace real classroom lighting.
questions: How many Wh do six A lamps use in 5 hours?
How many Wh do six B lamps use in the same time?
What is the difference, and why must saving energy not reduce lighting quality?

lessons.title: My school: grounds and building. Scale, plans, maps, Google Maps and models

exercises.label: A school plan drawn to scale
exercises.text: A plan shows an area from above using symbols. A scale of 1:100 means that 1 cm on the plan represents 100 cm, or 1 m, in real life. An imaginary classroom is 8 m long and 6 m wide. Draw its plan at 1:100 and mark the door, windows and two desks. Add a key explaining your symbols. Check that all lengths have been reduced by the same factor. You only need the given measurements, a ruler, a pencil and paper.
questions: How long and wide will the classroom be on the plan?
Why can you not reduce the length 100 times but the width only 10 times?
What should the key to a plan explain?

exercises.label: From a map to a model
exercises.text: A map covers an area, a plan shows a small area in more detail, and a model represents an object’s three-dimensional shape. Look at a map of the school neighbourhood in Google Maps or an image prepared by your teacher. Find the school building, a road and a green space. Use map directions to describe their positions relative to one another, without publishing your personal routes or addresses. Then sketch a cardboard school model and list its materials and assembly steps.
questions: How does a model differ from a plan?
Which three objects will you mark on the grounds plan?
Why might a satellite image differ from the area’s present appearance?

exercises.label: Investigating the learning space
exercises.text: A classroom audit is a systematic check using criteria chosen in advance. In a group, investigate one room: is there enough space to walk, can pupils see the board from different seats, are there reflections on the screen, and are materials easy to reach? Do not move heavy furniture or touch electrical equipment. Record factual observations separately from judgements. For example, “a backpack lies between the desks” is an observation, while “it is inconvenient here” is a judgement that needs explaining.
questions: Write four criteria for checking a classroom.
Give an observation without judgement words.
How can you check whether pupils in different seats notice the problem?

exercises.label: From evidence to a proposal
exercises.text: After the audit, choose one problem and suggest an achievable improvement. For each idea, identify evidence, resources and a way to test it. For example, if boxes cover shelf labels, suggest a new arrangement and larger labels. Agree on the change with the teacher, draw a sketch and compare the time needed to find an item before and after. Create a short infographic with three sections: “What we noticed”, “What we suggest” and “How we will test it”.
questions: What evidence supports your chosen problem?
What improvement can you make with available materials?
Which measure will you compare before and after the change?

exercises.label: Saving energy while keeping the benefit
exercises.text: Energy efficiency means achieving the required result with less energy. Reading in the dark to save energy is a poor idea because lighting must remain adequate. Compare lamps when they provide the same useful lighting. List five school actions: switch off unneeded lights, use daylight without glare, close doors to heated rooms, and choose other suitable solutions. For each action, explain which energy loss it reduces.
questions: How does energy efficiency differ from giving up lighting?
Which two actions can pupils take themselves?
Which changes need decisions by qualified adults?

exercises.label: Compare two operating schedules
exercises.text: In a practice problem, a 20 W light operates for 6 hours each day. After a habit changes, it is switched off for two hours when the room is empty. Daily energy use equals power multiplied by operating time. Calculate energy use before and after the change, then find the difference over five school days. Explain how switching off an unneeded device affects consumption. For a real investigation, use recorded readings supplied by your teacher.
questions: How many Wh did the light originally use each day?
How many Wh does it use in 4 hours?
How much energy is saved over 5 days?

exercises.label: A signal must be clear
exercises.text: A signalling system conveys a message using light, sound or pictures. For a learning model, agree that green means “the resource is being used appropriately”, yellow means “check the conditions”, and red means “tell an adult about a problem”. These meanings are your agreement for this model. Add labels and different symbols so the message is understandable without distinguishing colours. modules.title: Module 2. People and nature. Me in the Universe

lessons.title: Objects in the Universe. Optical instruments for observing the sky

exercises.label: Distinguishing objects in the Universe
exercises.text: A star emits its own light. A planet orbits a star and is seen mainly by reflected light. The Sun is a star, Earth is a planet, and the Moon is Earth’s natural satellite. An asteroid is a small rocky body, while a comet contains ice and dust and may develop a tail near the Sun. A galaxy contains a huge number of stars and other objects. Make cards for six kinds of celestial objects and write one distinguishing feature on each.
questions: Why can we see the Moon although it is not a star?
What is Earth’s place in the Solar System?
How does a galaxy differ from a single star?

exercises.label: Plan an observation of the sky
exercises.text: An optical telescope collects light from distant objects and helps reveal details. Binoculars can also be useful for observing the Moon. With your teacher, plan an evening observation: choose an accessible place, time, target and recording method. Draw the shape of the Moon’s visible part and record the date, time and cloud cover. If conditions do not allow observation, use prepared images. Never point a telescope or binoculars at the Sun: doing so can damage your eyesight.
questions: What should you record alongside a drawing of the Moon?
How does cloud cover affect observation?
Why do you need records from several observations to make comparisons?

lessons.title: The history of space exploration. Spacecraft and space stations

exercises.label: How people explored space
exercises.text: Space exploration includes different milestones. The first artificial Earth satellite reached orbit in 1957; Yuri Gagarin made the first human spaceflight in 1961; and humans first landed on the Moon during Apollo 11 in 1969. Make a timeline with these three events. Add separate cards for space mission tasks: observing Earth, exploring other worlds and conducting experiments. Explain why each event required a large team.
questions: How many years passed between the first satellite and the first human spaceflight?
How many years passed from 1961 to 1969?
Why can one person not prepare an entire space mission alone?

exercises.label: Choose a spacecraft for a mission
exercises.text: A launch vehicle helps carry a payload into space. An artificial satellite works in orbit; an interplanetary probe investigates distant objects; and a rover travels over another world’s surface. An orbital station can provide a place for a crew to live and conduct research. Choose one mission: image clouds above Earth, examine Martian soil or conduct a long experiment with a crew. Suggest a suitable spacecraft, two necessary devices and a way to send results to Earth.
questions: Which spacecraft best fits your chosen mission?
Why does a spacecraft need a power source?
What information will you send to the ground team?

exercises.label: Why protection is needed in space
exercises.text: Open space has no breathable air or adequate external pressure for a person. Radiation, temperature conditions and small particles also pose hazards. During a spacewalk, a spacesuit provides breathing gas, the required pressure and temperature control; it does not fully protect against all forms of space radiation. Draw a “hazard — protection” diagram and explain the roles of an airtight suit, communication and a safety tether.
questions: Why can ordinary warm clothing not replace a spacesuit?

exercises.label: Plan a crew’s day
exercises.text: On an orbital station, people and equipment experience microgravity because they move together in free fall around Earth. This does not mean Earth’s gravity has disappeared. The crew secures objects and exercises regularly to support muscles and bones. Plan a day including research, exercise, meals, communication and rest. Put six tasks in order, identify necessary equipment and explain why rest and exercise are as important as scientific work.

lessons.title: Space professions today and in the future

exercises.label: A space mission team
exercises.text: A space mission needs many specialists working together. An engineer designs the craft, a programmer develops control algorithms, an astronomer studies celestial objects, a doctor monitors crew health, a biologist plans experiments with living things, and an operator controls systems from Earth. Choose a mission observing plants on a station and map its team. For each role, write a task, the knowledge required and the information the specialist will share with colleagues.
questions: Why must the programmer communicate with the engineer?
What different data do the doctor and biologist collect?
Which two professions interest you most, and why?

exercises.label: A future profession: from an idea to requirements
exercises.text: Suggest a possible future profession, such as a lunar greenhouse grower or a repair-robot operator. This is a classroom prediction, so explain the conditions under which the work might be needed. Describe three duties, two useful school subjects and one teamwork skill. Write a short job advertisement. Include the problem the person will solve and a criterion for successful work. Compare your idea with an existing profession.
questions: How does your proposed profession differ from an existing one?
What knowledge can you start acquiring at school?

lessons.title: The history of flight. Forces in nature and technology

exercises.label: From balloons to aeroplanes
exercises.text: Balloons, gliders and powered aeroplanes use different technical solutions to rise and move. A balloon is supported by the buoyant force of air; in a hot-air balloon, the gas inside is less dense than the surrounding air. A glider’s wing produces lift while moving relative to air. A powered aeroplane has an engine that provides thrust. Make a short timeline of flight ideas: balloon, glider, aeroplane. For each one, write what supports it in the air and whether an engine is needed for thrust.

exercises.label: Four forces during flight
exercises.text: An aeroplane in flight experiences gravity downwards, lift from its wings, engine thrust and air resistance. In the simple case of straight, level flight at constant speed, lift balances gravity and thrust balances air resistance. Draw an aeroplane from the side and label four force arrows. lessons.title: Friction. What would happen if it disappeared?

exercises.imageAlt: A treaded shoe grips a path; a graphite pencil leaves a mark on paper.
exercises.label: Friction helps and hinders
exercises.text: Friction arises when surfaces interact and opposes their relative sliding or tendency to slide. Friction between shoes and the floor lets us push off while walking, and brakes slow a wheel. However, friction also causes wear and heating. Find six everyday examples: three where friction is useful and three where it is reduced. Explain the desired result for each. Imagine friction disappearing and describe how walking, writing with a pencil and braking would change.
questions: Why is it harder to start moving and stop on smooth ice?

exercises.imageAlt: The same box is pulled across a tabletop directly and on round pencil rollers.
exercises.label: Compare sliding and rolling
exercises.text: Place a light box on a table and pull it gently. Then place several identical round pencils underneath as rollers and repeat the movement. Do not use heavy objects or put your hands in front of the table edge. Compare the effort and describe what you notice: in many everyday situations, replacing sliding with rolling makes movement easier. For a fair comparison, keep the box, load, surface and distance the same. Repeat each version three times and do not treat guesses as measurements.
questions: Which condition are you changing?

exercises.label: Three types of friction: explore the diagram
exercises.text: Explore the diagram of static, sliding and rolling friction. Notice what happens where the surfaces touch. Classify the following situations and explain your choices.
exercises.imageAlt: Diagram: static friction — a box is pushed but does not slide; sliding friction — a sled slides over snow; rolling friction — a wheel rolls along a path.
questions: You push a wardrobe gently, but it stays in place. Which type of friction prevents sliding from starting?
A sled slides over snow and a suitcase travels on wheels. Name the type of friction in each situation.
Give your own example of each type of friction. Why do wheels often make a load easier to move?
exercises.solution: Wardrobe: static friction with the floor. Sled: sliding friction between runners and snow. Suitcase: rolling friction at the wheels. Static means no relative sliding at the contact, not necessarily that the whole object is motionless. In many everyday situations, rolling resistance is lower than sliding resistance.

exercises.label: Rebuses: decode words about friction
exercises.text: Solve the three picture rebuses. The label below each picture gives its word. A minus sign means remove the specified letters; a plus sign means join the remaining parts in order. Write all three answers.
exercises.imageAlt: Three rebuses: 1) FROG - OG + ICE - E + T + LION - L. 2) SLIDE - E + RING - R. 3) ROLL + RING - R.
questions: Which answer names the interaction involved in both walking and writing with a pencil?
Which two ways of moving are hidden in the other rebuses? Give one example of each.
exercises.solution: 1. FROG - OG = FR; ICE - E = IC; LION - L = ION; FR + IC + T + ION = FRICTION. 2. SLIDE - E = SLID; RING - R = ING; SLID + ING = SLIDING. 3. ROLL + (RING - R) = ROLLING. Examples: a sled slides; a ball rolls.

exercises.label: Simple machines around us
exercises.text: Simple machines help change the size or direction of an applied force. A lever turns around a pivot; an inclined plane lifts a load along a longer path; a fixed pulley changes the pulling direction. exercises.label: How a wing interacts with air
exercises.text: As a wing moves relative to air, the airflow around it changes: air is deflected and pressure above and below the wing may differ. This interaction produces lift. Lift depends on wing shape, area, airflow speed and angle of attack. The chord is an imaginary straight line from the front to the back of a wing section; the angle between it and the airflow is the angle of attack. Air particles do not have to meet again at the same time behind the wing. Draw a wing from the side, label airflow and lift, and explain the role of air in your own words.
